ov: Five stories from the 1890s that set Australian life, mateship and hardship in the bush against a sharp, often comic narrative voice: ‘The Drover’s Wife’, ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, ‘Shooting the Moon’, ‘Our Pipes’ and ‘The Loaded Dog’. Together they ask what real strength looks like when the bush is harsh, when communities are thin and when humour is a form of survival.
rub: Language, forms and features: the short story, the yarn, laconic dialogue, irony and the vernacular.
Challenging assumptions: the romantic “bush legend” is contested by realism and satire.
Agency and conformity: individual endurance against social expectations, and the rituals of mateship.
sum: In ‘The Drover’s Wife’, a woman alone with her children in a remote bush hut spends a night guarding them from a snake, drawing on memories of earlier hardships, floods, fire and isolation, while her husband is away droving. In ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, a narrator observes the funeral of an unknown drowned man, where the mourners’ clumsy rituals and dry humour reveal both indifference and a stubborn loyalty: they did not know him, but they knew he was a union man. ‘Shooting the Moon’ and ‘Our Pipes’ are Jack Mitchell’s yarns, told by swagmen camped under the moon: one about sneaking out of a pub without paying and meeting a generous publican, the other about a boy’s first pipe and the lengths he went to to hide it. In ‘The Loaded Dog’, three mates fishing with dynamite are chased by their own retriever, who runs into a crowded pub with a lit cartridge.
acts: A woman defends her children against a snake during a long night alone. Her son promises he will never become a drover.

cx: Henry Lawson (1867–1922) grew up in rural New South Wales in a poor family. His mother, Louisa Lawson, was a writer and early feminist, and the isolated, hard-working bush woman of ‘The Drover’s Wife’ is often connected to her experience. His own bouts with poverty and alcohol feed into the sympathy and dryness of his writing.

Lawson wrote for the Bulletin in the 1890s, when it championed a national, democratic “bush legend” of mateship and independence. Lawson both contributes to the legend and tests it with realism, irony and pity. The yarn, a spoken story told around the campfire, is an Australian oral form that he adapts to print.

The 1890s brought drought, bank crashes, the shearers’ strikes and the rise of the union movement. Unions gave workers solidarity, which is why the drovers in ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’ say of the stranger, “I knew he was a union man.” The colonies were not yet a federation (1901).

Isolated bush families, the harshness of women’s work, class divisions between squatters, shearers and swagmen, and the tension between rural and city life. Lawson draws attention to those whom history often ignores.
im: The snake and the fire in ‘The Drover’s Wife’: the snake is a physical threat; the fire is the mother’s vigil. At daybreak the “sickly daylight” fades the tension.
The sun and the cemetery in ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’: the harsh midday light removes any false sentiment (“the burial took place exactly at mid-day”).
The moon in ‘Shooting the Moon’ and ‘Our Pipes’: it is both the setting and the prompt for a yarn. It is described as “a big new copper boiler set on edge”, a comic and earthy image.
The yellow dog and the cartridge in ‘The Loaded Dog’: the image of an excited dog with a fuse spreading panic is the heart of the comedy.
th: People survive hardship through habit, humour and sheer stubbornness.

A.i: In his bush stories, Henry Lawson offers audiences opportunities to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability by quietly challenging the 1890s “bush legend” of the stoic, independent male. Through ‘The Drover’s Wife’, ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’ and ‘The Loaded Dog’, he suggests that strength is found in endurance, solidarity and humour, and that those most exposed to hardship often show the most courage. Lawson’s laconic, ironic voice invites us to see vulnerability as part of strength, not its opposite.
b: Lawson first challenges the assumption that bush strength belongs to men. In ‘The Drover’s Wife’, the description “His wife and children are left here alone” in the flat present tense establishes the family’s vulnerability, while the fragment “Bush all round – bush with no horizon” heightens isolation. Yet the woman responds with a stoical “No use fretting”, the clipped colloquial voice marking a strength that does not need display. By placing a mother at the centre of the bush story, Lawson dismantles the notion that courage is male.

Lawson also reveals how people display strength through small acts of loyalty. In ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, the narrator deflates sentimentality with the ironic statement, “I have left out the wattle – because it wasn’t there”, and the deadpan “It didn’t matter much – nothing does.” Yet when asked about the dead man, a drover replies, “I knew he was a union man.” The plain dialogue reveals a thin but real solidarity, a vulnerable kind of strength found in belonging to a group. Lawson thus questions the stereotype of the self-sufficient bushman.

Finally, humour exposes human weakness as a source of resilience. In ‘The Loaded Dog’, the narrator’s description of Tommy “smiling his broadest, longest, and reddest smile of amiability” uses a comic list to make the mates’ disaster funny, and the closing tease, “’El-lo, Da-a-ve! How’s the shin’ getting on?”, shows laughter turning embarrassment into belonging. The community’s humour does not deny vulnerability; it absorbs it.
A.c: Ultimately, Lawson invites audiences to reconsider what it means to be strong. By pairing vulnerability with endurance, loyalty and laughter, his stories suggest that strength is not independence but the ability to stand with others, and with oneself, in a harsh country.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis names the “assumption” (the bush legend) and the three stories chosen; each paragraph proves one idea; the quotes are short; technique (flat declarative, fragment, irony, comic list) is named with its effect; the conclusion offers a judgement.

B.i: In his short stories, Henry Lawson shows that strength and vulnerability go together. Through ‘The Drover’s Wife’ and ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, he challenges ideas about the bush.
b: In ‘The Drover’s Wife’, the mother is alone with her children, which makes her vulnerable. Lawson says, “Bush all round – bush with no horizon”, which shows she is isolated. But she says, “No use fretting”, which shows that she is strong. This shows that women can be strong in the bush.

In ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, the narrator says, “I have left out the wattle – because it wasn’t there.” This shows that he thinks the funeral is not as sad as it should be. The drover says, “I knew he was a union man”, which shows that the Union cares about its members.

In ‘The Loaded Dog’, the dog causes chaos with a cartridge. The narrator says the dog is “smiling his broadest, longest, and reddest smile of amiability.” This is funny and shows the mates are good at laughing at themselves.
B.c: In conclusion, Lawson shows that strength and vulnerability go together in the bush. His characters are strong because they keep going and have a sense of humour.
B.n: What to notice: a relevant argument and appropriate quotes, but each paragraph mostly retells. Techniques are rarely named, and the effect is explained generally. The question’s “assumptions” are only hinted at.

A.i: Through the particular lives of the drover’s wife, a funeral party of strangers and the mates of ‘The Loaded Dog’, Henry Lawson’s short stories enrich our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit as practical, communal and often comic. Writing in the 1890s, amid drought and economic hardship, Lawson avoids heroics. He shows endurance as habit, loyalty and humour, and invites audiences to honour lives that history often forgets.
b: Lawson represents endurance as quiet vigilance in ‘The Drover’s Wife’. The present-tense statement, “His wife and children are left here alone”, places the mother in permanent exposure, while the stoical “No use fretting” shows her refusal of self-pity. At the end, her son vows, “Mother, I won’t never go drovin’; blast me if I do!”, the vernacular speech revealing a child who has absorbed the cost of the bush. The final image of them sitting together as “the sickly daylight breaks over the bush” suggests survival without triumph, and the particular life of one woman deepens our understanding of the spirit’s endurance.

In ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, endurance becomes the strength of a community that barely knows its dead. The narrator refuses sentiment: “I have left out the wattle – because it wasn’t there”, and the bleak understatement “It didn’t matter much – nothing does” reflects how hardship dulls feeling. Yet the drover’s “I knew he was a union man” shows an enduring loyalty that survives beyond the person. The stranger’s life is particular in its anonymity, and his burial reveals how collective belonging sustains the spirit.

Finally, Lawson shows that humour is itself endurance. In ‘The Loaded Dog’, the comic list of Tommy “smiling his broadest, longest, and reddest smile of amiability” and the bushmen “trying to laugh without shrieking” turn near-catastrophe into laughter. The teasing call, “’El-lo, Da-a-ve!”, ensures that the story outlives the event, and teasing becomes belonging. In a harsh country, the capacity to laugh is shown to be as vital as the capacity to work.
A.c: Lawson’s representation of these particular lives therefore enriches our understanding of the human spirit’s endurance: it survives not through spectacular courage but through vigilance, loyalty and laughter, ordinary forces that make the bush bearable.
A.n: What to notice: “endurance” is defined (practical, communal, comic) and proved in three stories. “Particular lives” is named in each paragraph, techniques are specific, and the last sentence of each paragraph returns to the question.

B.i: In his short stories, Henry Lawson shows the endurance of the human spirit through the lives of the drover’s wife and the mates in ‘The Loaded Dog’. They face hardships but keep going.
b: In ‘The Drover’s Wife’, the mother is alone with her children. She says, “No use fretting.” This shows that she is strong and will not give up. Her son says, “I won’t never go drovin’”, which shows that he has seen how hard it is.

In ‘The Union Buries Its Dead’, the mourners do not know the dead man. The narrator says, “It didn’t matter much – nothing does.” This shows that they have got used to hardship. But the drover says, “I knew he was a union man”, which shows loyalty.
In ‘The Loaded Dog’, the mates are teased: “’El-lo, Da-a-ve! How’s the shin’ getting on?” This shows that humour helps people to cope.
B.c: In conclusion, Lawson shows the endurance of the human spirit through characters who keep going and find humour in difficult situations.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes and ideas, but the paragraphs mostly state what happens and what it “shows”. There is little analysis of technique, and the question’s “enriches our understanding” is not addressed.

fc: A spoken story told around a campfire or in a pub. Lawson adapts it in ‘Shooting the Moon’ and ‘Our Pipes’, where Jack Mitchell tells it.
A sentence fragment with repetition: “Bush all round – bush with no horizon”, creating isolation.
What is ironic about “I have left out the wattle – because it wasn’t there”?
The narrator mocks the clichés of funeral sentiment, so the story avoids false emotion.
What does the teasing at the end of ‘The Loaded Dog’ show?
Humour forms community; the joke outlives the disaster.
Which 1890s event makes the Union matter?
The rise of unions after the economic crash and shearers’ strikes; solidarity was a form of security.
